q-5998:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ $a=1,$ and $b=4.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{4}x-\frac{1}{x}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{4}x-\frac{1}{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+\frac{16}{{x}^{2}}+8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{{(\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{x}{4}+\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2})|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+\frac{1}{8}(4)^{2}]-[\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{1}{8}(1)^{2}] \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4+2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\frac{1}{8} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4+\frac{15}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-82616:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm \operatorname{arcsin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=\sqrt{2}-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x.$

q-82639:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+9x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=9x\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm 3\sqrt{x}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm 3\int \sqrt{x}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm 2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=-2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}.$

q-42153:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & 9 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & 9 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+3y=2 \\ 0x+0y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x+3y=2.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=2-3y,$ and the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2-3y \\ y=y\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2-3y \\ y\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-73751:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 & -5 \\ 2 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 & -5 \\ 2 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 \\ 2 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-2y=-1 \\ 0x+0y=4.\end{aligned}
$$

However, the final equation $0x+0y=4$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=4,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

q-126458:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $C$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=c+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $c$ is the position vector of $C.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $C(-1,0,4)$ and $D(-7,2,11)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{CD} \\  & =⟨-7,2,11⟩-⟨-1,0,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-6,2,7⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-162161:
We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
r=p+tv\,⟹\,r=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

and the vector equation of the  line segment $\overset{―}{PQ}$ is

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=3+1+0=4.
$$

q-130730:
The row operation applied to $X$ consists of multiplying a row by the number $\frac{1}{4}.$

When we do this, the determinant is multiplied by the same number. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Y) & =\frac{1}{4}det(X) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (-48) \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130729:
The row operation applied to $X$ consists of multiplying a row by the number $-\frac{4}{15}.$

When we do this, the determinant is multiplied by the same number. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Y) & =-\frac{4}{15}det(X) \\  & =-\frac{4}{15}\cdot (-60) \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130740:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot B)={k}^{n}\cdot det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=5$ and $n=2.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(5B) & ={5}^{2}\cdot det(B) \\  & =25\cdot (-4) \\  & =-100.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130739:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot Y)={k}^{n}\cdot det(Y).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=-4$ and $n=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(-4Y) & =(-4)^{3}\cdot det(Y) \\  & =-64\cdot 2 \\  & =-128.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we only have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one. Consequently, we get

$$
